source.version_note: Supplied 2022 early-view article, first online 5 August 2022; subsequently Journal of Consumer Behaviour 22(2):455–467, March 2023. Filename uses issue year; these are versions of one work.
source.verification_method: All thirteen pages read, including the complete four-scenario appendix, literature table, results and references. Conceptual diagram, result chart and inconsistent coefficients on PDF pages 6–8 visually checked. Crossref verifies online/issue dates and bibliography. Basic F/t-tail and coefficient-product checks use the printed inputs, not a reproduction of raw data.

citation.title: Do not put the blame on me: Asymmetric responses to service outcome with autonomous vehicles versus human agents
citation.venue: Journal of Consumer Behaviour; online 2022, issue 22(2):455–467 (2023)

reading.source_scope_note: Three scenario experiments on imagined taxi service, plus a pretest. Measures human customer satisfaction, perceived fault and competence, not actual autonomous-driving safety, machine ability, legal liability or behavior of an AI. Mediators are measured rather than independently randomized, and material reporting discrepancies limit precise conclusions.
access_limits: Entire supplied early-view PDF, tables, figures and appendix read. No raw data, code or later corrected/final text was obtained; data are described as available from the author on request, and no contact was made.
Original cited studies and books remain secondary. Crossref metadata and one deposited abstract are explicitly limited verification, not additional complete-paper reads.

study.samples: Pretest 111 US MTurk workers; Study 1 convenience sample 201 European-university students/former students; Study 2 118 US MTurk workers; Study 3 124 university students/former students. Main-study Ns sum to 443, plus pretest 111 gives 554 reported participation instances, not verified unique people across stages. Recruitment attrition and exclusions are not fully detailed.
study.scenarios: Study 1 randomized 2 × 2 human/AV and negative/positive service. Appendix: same vacation meeting scenario, negative arrival 30 minutes late and destination 40 minutes late; positive pickup on time and destination five minutes early. Thus positive is not merely an exactly-on-time mirror of the negative condition. AV scenarios add a safety/no-human-input definition, a potential framing confound.
study.study1: Satisfaction interaction F(1,197)=10.84, p=.001. Negative means AV 2.79 versus human 2.02, contrast F=8.86, p=.003. Positive means AV 5.56 versus human 5.98, F=2.75 with printed p=.99; ordinary F(1,197) tail is approximately .09885. This remains nonsignificant at .05 but is not equivalence or zero difference.
study.study2: Failure-only comparison, satisfaction plus a two-item perceived-blame index mixing blameworthiness and causal contribution. Human→blame b=.77; blame→satisfaction b=−.24; adjusted direct b=.06, nonsignificant; indirect b=−.18, CI [−.34,−.06]. These are measured-mediator paths, not proof of complete causal mediation.
study.study3: Failure-only comparison, same satisfaction/blame plus one competence item. The stated competence item compares the human agent with the company owning the AV, not the AV itself. Reverse-coded so higher means more competent. Reported human→competence .72; competence→blame .40; human→blame .50; blame→satisfaction −.28; competence→satisfaction .05, nonsignificant; human adjusted direct→satisfaction +.56, significant.
study.inconsistent_mediation: Study 3's negative indirect paths (serial −.08, blame-only −.14) coexist with a larger positive direct effect +.56 and positive competence-only indirect about +.04. Under ordinary same-sample linear PROCESS decomposition, printed rounded paths imply total human-minus-AV satisfaction about +.38, not the repeatedly claimed overall AV satisfaction advantage. No raw total effect is supplied to resolve this conflict.
study.competence_scope: The paper defines perceived competence as having the skills, knowledge and capabilities to deliver the service. Actual competence, expectations, intention, flexibility, control, manufacturer competence and vehicle competence are not interchangeable; only a single mixed-target perception item is used in Study 3.
study.outcome_scope: All ratings follow imagined episodes. No actual taxi choice, payment, complaint, forgiveness, accident response, safety performance or legal sanction is observed. Three experiments in one article are not three independent source papers.

summary: Add perceived competence and blame attribution with explicit perception/measurement boundaries. Enrich existing human–robot judgment asymmetry rather than creating another algorithmic-forgiveness synonym; keep satisfaction separate from outrage, aversion and unjust human scapegoating.

findings.definition: A judgment that an agent or organization has the skills, knowledge and capabilities needed to perform a task adequately.
findings.origin: Social perception / consumer and human–AI interaction research
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit human perception construct with one-item evidence in an imagined taxi failure; company-versus-vehicle wording and reporting conflicts limit mechanism claims
findings.ai_proposal: Measure beliefs about a system's capability separately from benchmarked performance, reliability and confidence. Identify the target precisely: model, full service, human operator or company. Test whether descriptions and explanations calibrate expectations rather than merely increase apparent expertise, and verify actual performance on the task before consequential delegation.
findings.novelty_rationale: An evaluator's belief about another entity's ability differs from apparent competence masking inconsistent support needs, a person's self-efficacy, trustworthiness or actual measured performance. It can be accurate or inaccurate and is not inherently a harmful bias.

evidence.quote: service provider possesses the required skills
service robot competence, defined as robot's ability
human agent vs. the company that owns

findings.evidence_scope: The paper explicitly defines perceived provider competence and measures it in Study 3, with humans rated higher than the AV-company comparison. A positive competence–blame coefficient is conditional association within a measured-mediator model. It does not establish actual competence, a direct manipulation of perceived ability or that lowering perceived competence improves overall satisfaction.
findings.boundary: Specify whose competence and in which task. A vehicle, owning company, human driver and complete service are different targets. Perceived competence, felt warmth, moral agency, reliability and actual skill differ. Accurate disclosure of limits is appropriate; cultivating an impression of incompetence to escape accountability is not a supported recommendation.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human post-vignette judgments measured with a two-item index mixing fault and causation; no actual liability decision or AI internal moral judgment demonstrated
findings.ai_proposal: When explaining a failure, distinguish causal contribution, control, knowledge, foreseeability, role obligations and deserved censure. Identify operator, developer, deploying organization and technical system without treating a product label as a substitute for evidence. Test whether matched human/AI descriptions change attributed fault while keeping authority and available alternatives explicit.
findings.novelty_rationale: General attribution of fault is a broader evaluative act than the existing specific reversal, credit/blame asymmetry, scapegoating or crumple-zone patterns. It can be justified and does not imply an unfair shift. Keep those narrower effects separate rather than use them for every negative judgment.

evidence.quote: perceived less blame worthy for the negative service outcome

findings.evidence_scope: Studies 2/3 measure participants' attributed blameworthiness and causal contribution for a delayed taxi. Human conditions receive more blame in the reported models; perceived blame associates negatively with satisfaction. The two-item index does not separate causal responsibility from deserved moral/legal blame, and indirect paths do not establish causation.
findings.boundary: Causation alone does not settle blameworthiness or liability. Blame can be warranted; identifying a real human or institutional duty is not scapegoating. A system's low perceived agency does not remove operator/deployer obligations, and a simulation does not establish a legal standard or prove responsibility should move to any single party.

findings.definition: Differences in moral evaluations of otherwise matched decisions attributed to human versus artificial agents.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds scoped human/AV fault judgments for an ordinary service failure rather than creating a new forgiveness or underreaction label for the same comparison.

evidence.quote: significant increase of perceived blame for the human agent condition

findings.evidence_scope: Failure-only studies report higher human blame, and Study 1 reports an agent × outcome satisfaction interaction. This is context-dependent human rating evidence, not proof of a universally more forgiving response to AI. Study 3's competence item changes target to owning company and its adjusted direct satisfaction coefficient favors humans, limiting the broad AV-advantage interpretation.
findings.boundary: Delayed service differs from fatal accidents, joint supervision or intentional wrongdoing. Match role, control, competence information and target identity before attributing a difference to agent type alone. Null positive-outcome contrast is not evidence of equivalence or absence of a positive response.

findings.definition: Experiencing or expressing less moral outrage over wrongdoing attributed to an algorithm than over comparable wrongdoing attributed to a human.
findings.novelty_rationale: Avoids equating satisfaction after delay and a two-item blame index with directly measured moral outrage.

evidence.quote: Following the scenario, we measured customer satisfaction

findings.evidence_scope: The study measures satisfaction, blame and competence rather than a moral-outrage scale or expressive response. Boundary-only relation; do not count as a direct outrage experiment.
findings.boundary: Less dissatisfaction or blame need not mean less moral outrage, justified forgiveness or acceptance of wrongdoing. These constructs and their normative evaluation require separate measurement.

findings.definition: A human operator receives disproportionate blame for an automated system's failure despite limited control over the outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: The article invokes a human liability sponge as a possible account, but the experiment does not show blame assigned beyond actual control.

evidence.quote: act like “liability sponge”, absorbing all responsibility

findings.evidence_scope: Liability-sponge discussion is secondary and speculative. A human driver in a different condition is not a limited-control operator of the AV, and the study does not measure blame assigned to AV programmers or a supervising human. Boundary-only, not direct evidence of a crumple zone.
findings.boundary: More blame for a human performing a task than for a vehicle does not by itself establish unjust blame for a human supervisor. Actual control, role obligations and institutional responsibility must be assessed independently.

findings.definition: Weighting negative cues in the prompt or context more than equivalent positive ones, skewing its read and its output.
findings.novelty_rationale: Separates an agent-type interaction by outcome valence from a demonstrated general negative-information weighting mechanism.

evidence.quote: reacting differently to positive versus negative perceptions

findings.evidence_scope: Negativity/prospect theory motivate the hypotheses. The experiment compares a substantial delay with an on-time pickup/five-minute-early arrival, without equating magnitudes or an expected-value reference point. It does not independently identify negativity bias or loss aversion.
findings.boundary: Different reactions to unequal outcomes can be warranted. A significant agent × valence interaction is not a calibrated loss/gain asymmetry or proof that negative information is intrinsically more informative.

methodological_limits: Convenience university samples and MTurk participants are not representative of travelers or actual AV users. Claims that students are less taxi-experienced than adults are explanations offered without an experience measure or controlled comparison.

Hypothetical taxi delays in one context do not generalize automatically to severe crashes, medical harms, deliberate misconduct or other transportation roles. Current autonomous-driving safety superiority is not tested; the introduction's broad 90%-human-error argument does not show 90% of crashes would be prevented.

The positive appendix scenario includes arrival five minutes early; the negative is 30/40 minutes late. Outcome intensity, reference point and expectations are not matched. AV descriptions uniquely add a capability-to-move-safely definition, which may affect perceived reliability or blame.

Pretest human-identification mean 3.90 on a 1-human/7-AV scale is near the midpoint; significant between-group separation is not proof that every participant identified the manipulation correctly. Negative outcome mean 3.96 is also near neutral. Main-study comprehension checks and attrition are not fully reported.

Study 1's printed cell SDs .17–.19 conflict with marginal SDs .97/1.58; the small values could be standard errors but are labeled SD and figure error bars are not defined. Raw output is needed before using standardized effects or precision.
Study 1 positive contrast F(1,197)=2.75 has ordinary p≈.09885, not .99. Either remains nonsignificant at .05, which does not demonstrate equality or justify the word only as a universal claim.

Study 2 t=3.05 with approximately 116 residual df implies two-sided p≈.00284 rather than the printed .03. Small coefficient/SE/t discrepancies can arise from rounding, but this tenfold p mismatch is larger. Preserve the discrepancy instead of silently replacing reported data.

Study 3 prints blame→satisfaction b=−.28, SE=.47, t=−5.96. These cannot all hold: |b/SE|≈.596. SE=.047 would be plausible but is only a conjecture, not an authorized source correction. Several other rounded b/SE/t pairs warrant output verification.

Study 3's competence item explicitly compares human driver versus company owning the AV. This changes both entity and aggregation level; do not summarize it as a clean measurement that the vehicle itself is less competent.

The blame scale combines deserved blame and causal contribution, which can differ. A significant correlation between two items is not discriminant validity. One competence item does not distinguish technical, social, moral or adaptive ability.

Randomizing agent type can support a vignette-condition effect but does not randomize competence or blame. Same-session measured mediation cannot rule out confounding, reverse inference, expectations or overlapping evaluative judgments. A nonsignificant direct path does not establish complete causal mediation.

Study 3 is inconsistent mediation: a positive adjusted direct effect +.56 opposes negative indirect paths. Adding the printed path products yields a positive approximate total human advantage .375, whereas the conclusion repeats an AV satisfaction advantage. Raw total-effect and coding output are required; the discrepancy is not repaired by reversing labels or selecting only favorable paths.

Study 1 provides an actual interaction test. Studies 2/3 exclude positive outcomes, so they cannot independently replicate the valence interaction or establish that the proposed mediators operate only after failures.

No preregistration, power analysis, bootstrap resample count or multiple-comparison adjustment is specified in the supplied article. Repeated experiments within one article are one source identity, not multiple independently published papers.

The managerial advice to avoid enhancing perceived competence exceeds the design: neither interface design nor competence expectations are experimentally manipulated. Underselling competence to reduce blame and emphasizing hedonic reviews are not validated ethical interventions or evidence of safer services.

Speeding up after delay is an illustrative discussion example, not an acceptable safety prescription. Reduced dissatisfaction does not justify compromising traffic safety, suppressing failures, manipulating reviews or shifting accountability.

Table 1's Erskine row describes blog choice and influence despite citing an AV acceptance paper. Deposited abstract metadata confirms the cited paper instead studies UTAUT2 attitudes to AVs. Original full text remains unread; the unrelated row is not imported as a research finding.

source_corrections.reliable_correction: Record first-online publication 5 August 2022 and later March 2023 issue 22(2):455–467. Both dates describe one work; do not count versions as separate papers or arbitrarily replace all 2023 issue citations.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Crossref online/print metadata and supplied early-view title/citation blocks.

source_corrections.location: Erskine et al. reference, PDF page 11; Table 1 row on page 2
source_corrections.problem: Reference pages printed 83–894 instead of 883–894; key-findings row talks about blogs rather than the cited autonomous-vehicle study.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Journal of Consumer Marketing 37(7):883–894, DOI 10.1108/JCM-10-2019-3441. Deposited abstract describes an N=1,154 UTAUT2 AV study with performance/effort expectancy, social influence and hedonic motivation; do not use the unrelated blog summary.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Bibliographic metadata and deposited abstract only; not a full reading or replication of Erskine et al.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Human/AI blame can reverse with role and context. A delay vignette's greater human blame does not override Mei's role-dependent results or establish a universal algorithmic forgiveness principle.

Perceived ability is not actual capacity, and responsibility labels are not a legal rule. A true crumple-zone claim requires mismatch between blame and feasible control, not simply a human/AV contrast.

Target identity and source provenance matter. Believing advice represents doctors when it derives from nonexperts and rating a company as if it were a vehicle are different construct/provenance problems; fluent summaries should preserve them.

Measured mediators and a disappearing direct p-value do not prove a complete causal process. This paper further shows why direct, indirect and total paths must all be checked before describing the overall outcome.

deferred.reason: Interpretive labels for context-specific existing human/robot asymmetry; forgiveness, warrantedness and actual behavioral acceptance are not directly measured. Do not add synonym entries.
Descriptive interaction label, not a uniquely identified general negativity/loss-aversion mechanism. Existing asymmetry entries and the review retain the result without another near-duplicate.
Service classifications, not additional psychological behaviors. The current experiments test imagined delayed outcome failure, not an independent process-versus-outcome manipulation.
Measured serial mediation, mixed-target competence question, contradictory direct/total implications and no competence intervention make this causal slogan unreliable.
Background theory or discussion extrapolation. Satisfaction and blame are not actual service choice, and no limited-control human overseeing the AV is assigned blame here.

limitations: Two perception/judgment concepts added; one existing asymmetry strengthened and three boundary-only sources excluded from direct paper counts. Numerical discrepancies remain visible; no guessed raw-data repair, current safety/clinical/legal conclusion, marketing endorsement or new normative edges.
